title: Think like a product manager: outcomes, risks and tests

say: Think like a product manager: outcomes, risks and tests.

say: The product manager, or PM, is the person whose job is to reduce that danger. She does not usually write the code or draw the screens.

say: By the end of this module you will frame a product problem as an outcome, a set of risks and a hypothesis you can test.

say: An output is something the team ships: a new screen, a feature, a release. Outputs are easy to count, so weak teams celebrate them.

An outcome is a change in what people do that matters to the business. Here is a simple test. If you can tick it off on release day, it is an output. If you must wait and watch user behaviour, it is an outcome.
A feature nobody uses is cost without value.
Every idea carries four risks. Value: will customers choose to use it? The PM leads here.

panel.heading: The four big product risks
items: Viability: does it work for us? (PM)

say: Usability: can users figure it out? The designer leads.

panel.heading: The four big product risks
items: Viability: does it work for us? (PM)

say: Feasibility: can our engineers build it with the time and skills we have?

panel.heading: The four big product risks
items: Viability: does it work for us? (PM)

say: Viability: does it work for legal, finance, support and partners? The PM owns this too. An idea is ready only with evidence on all four.

panel.heading: The four big product risks
items: Viability: does it work for us? (PM)

say: Here is a worked example. Amaka is PM for a savings app used by market traders in Lagos. A director wants traders to lock savings for 90 days for a higher rate.
On value, 6 of the last 40 support chats asked about fixed savings. That is a signal, not proof.

The ledger can hold end dates. A first version is about two weeks of work.
Finance must confirm the higher rate. Compliance must check the licence.

say: Step one. Write a problem statement: the user, the situation and what it costs them today, without naming a feature.

say: Step two. Write a hypothesis, a belief you can prove wrong, with a measurable signal and a time limit.

say: Step three. Design an MVP, a minimum viable product. It is the smallest test that teaches you something, not a broken cheap product. It may be just a WhatsApp number or a Google Form.

panel.rule: Write your success signal before the test starts.

say: Bisi runs product for a logistics start-up in Ibadan. The founder wants a full tracking app. Bisi tests a cheaper idea first: an SMS at pickup and at delivery, sent by hand to 20 sellers for four weeks.

panel.heading: Bisi tests before building an app
left: Founder wants a full tracking app
right: Manual SMS at pickup and delivery

say: Queries fall from about 300 a week to about 120. That is a 60% drop with no code written. Only now does she ask engineering to automate the messages.

say: Many users have entry-level phones, costly data and patchy signal. Run every major feature through this check.
Does it work on entry-level Android and survive a dropped network? Can people reach it by USSD, SMS or WhatsApp? Does it build trust, in simple language?
And check the licence and data rules. Under Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023, collect only what you need.

To remember. Measure outcomes, not just outputs. Check every idea for all four risks. Start with the problem, not a feature. Write your signal and time limit before you test. And keep your MVP as small as possible.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Problem first, without naming a feature
Signal and time limit written before the test
An MVP is the smallest test, not a broken product

say: Now practise. Run the four-risk check on a feature you have seen requested. Write your first problem, hypothesis and MVP. Score an app you know on the context checklist, and read two real PM job adverts.
Keep your notes for your capstone, and continue with the lessons below.
